Chapter 4. The Persistence of White Supremacy.
As the administration stepped into its second term, you could really feel the country’s divisions getting harder to ignore. Remember that sense of hope from the early years? It started to fade, replaced by this growing unease. All across cities in America, you’d see protests breaking out—sparked by police violence and the heartbreaking deaths of unarmed Black men and women. Old wounds that had never truly healed were ripped open yet again.
For so many people, these moments were a painful reminder: our history isn’t just about moving forward. The legacy of white supremacy isn’t some distant memory—it’s right here, shaping life today, sometimes in ways you can see, other times in ways that are hidden. Think about it: laws, policies, even the unspoken rules we live by. They all work together to keep things pretty much the same.
Imagine a college student, just starting to see how deep systemic racism runs. She might suddenly find herself questioning everything she’s ever believed. All those stories about hard work leading to success, about America being a land of equal opportunity—they start to sound hollow. And it’s not just a feeling. She can see it all around: neighborhoods divided by race and class, schools that barely provide for the kids who need help the most, and a justice system that seems anything but just.
Every time there’s been progress, there’s always been backlash. Now, it was louder than ever. Political leaders and media voices stoked fears, warning that the country was changing too fast, that the old way of life was slipping away. The election of a Black president didn’t heal the nation’s divisions—it showed just how deep those cracks really were.
For anyone who hoped this administration would be a true turning point, reality hit hard. White supremacy wasn’t going to just disappear. It adapted. It found new ways to show up, new ways to push back. The fight for equality was never a straight path—it was a constant struggle, with battles happening everywhere, all the time.
And right in the middle of all this, the writer kept wrestling with his own role in the story. He came to realize, fighting white supremacy isn’t just about new laws or different leaders. It’s about changing how we see ourselves, and each other. It’s about telling the truth—even when it hurts. It’s about not settling for easy answers, but digging deeper, demanding a real reckoning with our country’s past.
The events of those years made one thing crystal clear: the work isn’t done. The promise of a fair and just society still feels just out of reach. But you know what? The struggle itself—the refusal to give up—is proof of just how resilient and determined people can be.
